planting.note: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; largely deer-resistant and low-maintenance once established, like its parent Karl Foerster.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. A golden-variegated sport of the industry-standard Karl Foerster, Eldorado was discovered by growers in Washington State and shares its parent's strictly upright, non-flopping habit while adding a bright yellow stripe down the center of each narrow green leaf. Slender purplish flower spikes rise above the foliage in midsummer and mature to a rich wheat tone that persists through winter, reaching up to 5-6 feet in bloom. As a sterile hybrid it produces no viable seed, so it spreads only by slowly expanding clump and poses no self-seeding concerns.

planting.note: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; tolerates heat, drought, poor soil, and heavy clay with minimal care.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, and cut back in late winter before new growth begins. Twilight Zone stands out among little bluestem selections for its iridescent, silvery-mauve foliage that develops through midsummer and deepens toward rich purple tones as autumn arrives. New growth in spring emerges a cool blue-green before taking on its signature pastel coloring, giving the upright, columnar clump a shifting, almost metallic appearance across the season. Fluffy silver-white seed heads follow the narrow blue-toned foliage in fall, adding textural contrast and catching low autumn light. Native to North American prairies, it thrives in lean soil and tolerates heat, drought, poor soil, and heavy clay with minimal care.

planting.note: Plant in poor, rocky, or sandy well-drained soil in full sun; needs little supplemental water once established, well suited to xeriscaping.

directions: Plant in poor, rocky, or sandy well-drained soil in full sun, where it needs little supplemental water once established. Selected from the popular cultivar The Blues for its notably compact, non-flopping habit, Jazz forms a tight upright clump of narrow blue-green foliage that stays shorter and sturdier than most little bluestem selections. Purplish-bronze flower spikes appear in late summer, followed by fluffy silvery-white seed heads that persist into early winter and catch backlight beautifully. The blue-green blades shift to vivid red, orange, and purple tones with the first cool nights of fall, giving the plant strong multi-season interest in a smaller footprint, well suited to xeriscaping and small-space native plantings.

planting.note: Plant in average garden loam to wet or clay ground in full sun; needs minimal irrigation once established.

directions: Plant in average garden loam to wet or clay ground in full sun; tolerates a wide range of soils and needs minimal irrigation once established. Prairie Sky is prized among switchgrass cultivars for its strongly powder-blue foliage, a color it holds from spring through summer before shifting to soft yellow and then tan in late fall. Its columnar, strictly upright habit resembles the popular cultivar Heavy Metal but grows taller and bluer, sending up airy, dark rusty-red flower panicles above the foliage from late summer into fall that persist as a shimmering seed cloud through winter. Use it in mass plantings, screens, or naturalistic borders where its blue color and vertical form provide strong contrast to green-leaved perennials.

planting.note: Plant in full sun and average to lean, well-drained soil; established plants are drought- and salt-tolerant and need little maintenance beyond an early spring cutback.

directions: Plant in full sun in average to lean, well-drained soil, since established plants are drought- and salt-tolerant and need little maintenance beyond an early spring cutback. Introduced by German breeder Karl Foerster in the late 1960s, Rotstrahlbusch is one of the older switchgrass selections grown for reliably early and intense red coloring, with leaf tips flushing red by midsummer well before the burgundy fall color typical of most switchgrass cultivars. It is shorter and finer-textured than the wild species, forming a dense upright clump topped by airy, reddish-tinged seed heads in late summer that fade to beige through winter. The strong, non-flopping habit and compact size make it useful in smaller borders where taller switchgrass cultivars would overwhelm the planting.
